claim: βC1 interacts with NbATG8f in yeast
source: SKY48 yeast strains containing AD-NbATG8f transformed with BD-βC1 or BD (control) were grown on Leu- selection plates at 28°C for 4 d. The positive interaction was indicated by the blue colony formation on X-gal-containing galactose (Gala) and raffinose (Raf) but not on plates containing glucose (Glu).
evidence: Yeast two-hybrid assay showing blue colony formation indicates protein-protein interaction between βC1 and NbATG8f, as shown in Figure 1A

claim: NbATG8f interacts with βC1 in vitro
source: The total soluble proteins of E. coli expressing NbATG8f-6×His were incubated with GST-βC1 or GST-βC1V32A immobilized on glutathione-sepharose beads and monitored by anti-His antibody.
evidence: GST pull-down assay demonstrates direct physical interaction between purified proteins in vitro, as shown in Figure 1B

claim: βC1V32A does not interact with NbATG8f in vitro
source: The total soluble proteins of E. coli expressing NbATG8f-6×His were incubated with GST-βC1 or GST-βC1V32A immobilized on glutathione-sepharose beads and monitored by anti-His antibody.
evidence: GST pull-down assay shows no interaction between βC1V32A mutant and NbATG8f, as shown in Figure 1B

claim: βC1 was co-immunoprecipitated with NbATG8f in plant cells
source: GFP-NbATG8f was transiently co-expressed with and HA-βC1 or its mutant HA-βC1V32A in N. benthamiana leaves. At 60 hr post agroinfiltration (hpi), leaf lysates were immunoprecipitated with anti-GFP beads and then the precipitants were assessed by immunoblotting (IB) using anti-HA (upper panel) or anti-GFP antibodies (middle panel).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiment demonstrates in vivo interaction in plant cells, as shown in Figure 1C

claim: βC1V32A was not co-immunoprecipitated with NbATG8f in plant cells
source: GFP-NbATG8f was transiently co-expressed with and HA-βC1 or its mutant HA-βC1V32A in N. benthamiana leaves. At 60 hr post agroinfiltration (hpi), leaf lysates were immunoprecipitated with anti-GFP beads and then the precipitants were assessed by immunoblotting (IB) using anti-HA (upper panel) or anti-GFP antibodies (middle panel).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiment shows no interaction between βC1V32A mutant and NbATG8f in plant cells, as shown in Figure 1C

claim: An 11-amino acid motif from residue 30 to 40 of βC1 is necessary for its interaction with NbATG8f
source: Moreover, we identified an 11-amino acid motif from residue 30 to 40 of βC1 that is necessary for its interaction with NbATG8f (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Yeast two-hybrid assays with truncated mutants of βC1 identified the specific region required for interaction, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A positive interaction between nYFP-βC1 and cYFP-NbATG8f was observed in both the cytoplasm and vacuoles of plant cells
source: A positive interaction between nYFP-βC1 and cYFP-NbATG8f was observed in both the cytoplasm and vacuoles of plant cells, as indicated by the presence of yellow fluorescence (Figure 1D).
evidence: BiFC assay shows yellow fluorescence in cytoplasm and vacuoles indicating protein interaction in these subcellular locations, as shown in Figure 1D

claim: No interaction was detected between nYFP-βC1V32A and cYFP-NbATG8f
source: However, no such interaction was detected between nYFP-βC1V32A and cYFP-NbATG8f (Figure 1D), although all constructs were successfully expressed (Figure 1E).
evidence: BiFC assay shows no yellow fluorescence for the βC1V32A mutant, indicating loss of interaction, as shown in Figure 1D

claim: The βC1–NbATG8f interaction localizes to vacuoles with Brownian motion
source: We further confirmed the vacuolar localization of the βC1–NbATG8f interaction by performing time-lapse observations of mesophyll cells by confocal microscopy, which revealed Brownian motion of fluorescent punctate structures within the central vacuole (Video 1).
evidence: Time-lapse confocal microscopy shows Brownian motion of fluorescent puncta in vacuoles, confirming vacuolar localization, as shown in Video 1

claim: YFP-βC1 co-localized with GFP-NbATG8f-positive bodies in both the cytoplasm and central vacuoles
source: In addition, we found that YFP-βC1, but not YFP-βC1V32A, co-localized with GFP-NbATG8f-positive bodies in both the cytoplasm and central vacuoles of mesophyll cells of N. benthamiana leaf tissue, as revealed by confocal microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Confocal microscopy shows co-localization of YFP-βC1 with GFP-NbATG8f in cytoplasm and vacuoles, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: YFP-βC1V32A did not co-localize with GFP-NbATG8f-positive bodies
source: In addition, we found that YFP-βC1, but not YFP-βC1V32A, co-localized with GFP-NbATG8f-positive bodies in both the cytoplasm and central vacuoles of mesophyll cells of N. benthamiana leaf tissue, as revealed by confocal microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Confocal microscopy shows no co-localization of YFP-βC1V32A with GFP-NbATG8f, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The V32 residue is essential for the βC1–NbATG8f interaction
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that βC1 specifically interacts with NbATG8s and the V32 residue is essential for the βC1–NbATG8f interaction.
evidence: Multiple experimental approaches (yeast two-hybrid, GST pull-down, co-IP, BiFC) all show that V32A mutation abolishes the interaction

claim: mRNA levels of NbATG2, NbATG3, NbATG5, and NbATG7 were upregulated during CLCuMuV infection
source: First, we performed quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis, finding that mRNA levels of NbATG2, NbATG3, NbATG5, and NbATG7 were upregulated during the infection of plants with CLCuMuV (CA) plus CLCuMuB (β) (hereafter referred to as CLCuMuV infection or CA+β) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qRT-PCR data shows increased mRNA levels of multiple ATG genes during viral infection, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: CLCuMuV infection increased the number of autophagosomes in N. benthamiana plants
source: In N. benthamiana plants infected with CA+β, we observed increased numbers of autophagosomes (represented by CFP-NbATG8f puncta) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Confocal microscopy quantification shows increased CFP-NbATG8f puncta in infected plants, as shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: CLCuMuV infection increased the number of autophagic structures in infected cells
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that viral infection increased the number of autophagic structures in infected cells (Figure 2C,D) compared to the control.
evidence: TEM images show increased autophagic bodies in vacuoles of virus-infected cells, as shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: CLCuMuV infection reduced the protein level of NbJoka2
source: Indeed, we found that CLCuMuV infection (CA+β) reduced the protein level of NbJoka2, although it did not change mRNA level of NbJoka2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that viral infection enhances autophagic flux.
evidence: Western blot shows reduced NbJoka2 protein levels in infected plants, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: CLCuMuV infection did not change mRNA level of NbJoka2
source: Indeed, we found that CLCuMuV infection (CA+β) reduced the protein level of NbJoka2, although it did not change mRNA level of NbJoka2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that viral infection enhances autophagic flux.
evidence: qRT-PCR shows no change in NbJoka2 mRNA levels in infected plants, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: CLCuMuV infection enhances autophagic flux
source: Indeed, we found that CLCuMuV infection (CA+β) reduced the protein level of NbJoka2, although it did not change mRNA level of NbJoka2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that viral infection enhances autophagic flux.
evidence: Reduction in Joka2 protein without change in mRNA indicates increased autophagy-mediated degradation, which is a measure of autophagic flux

claim: CLCuMuV infection induces autophagy
source: These data demonstrate that CLCuMuV infection induces autophagy.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence including increased ATG gene expression, increased autophagosomes, increased autophagic structures, and enhanced autophagic flux all support this conclusion

claim: The mRNA levels of NbATG5 and NbATG7 were significantly reduced by gene-specific VIGS
source: Compared to non-silenced control plants, the mRNA levels of NbATG5 and NbATG7 were significantly reduced by gene-specific VIGS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), whereas we observed no obvious differences in TRV RNA levels between ATG5-silenced plants, ATG7-silenced plants, and control plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR shows reduced mRNA levels of target genes in VIGS plants, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Autophagy was blocked in ATG5- and ATG7-silenced plants
source: In addition, autophagy was blocked in ATG5- and ATG7-silenced plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Confocal microscopy quantification shows reduced autophagic puncta in ATG5- and ATG7-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: CLCuMuV infection had no effect on TRV-mediated VIGS
source: It is worth noting that CLCuMuV infection had no effect on TRV-mediated VIGS (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: PDS silencing still caused bleached phenotype in CLCuMuV-infected plants, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Leaf curl symptoms caused by viral infection were much more severe in ATG5- and ATG7-silenced plants compared to control plants
source: We observed that the leaf curl symptoms caused by viral infection were much more severe and appeared 3 days earlier (Figure 3A,B), and CLCuMuV DNA levels were significantly higher in ATG5- and ATG7- silenced plants compared to control plants (Figure 3C).
evidence: Visual observation and symptom incidence data show more severe symptoms in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Leaf curl symptoms appeared 3 days earlier in ATG5- and ATG7-silenced plants
source: We observed that the leaf curl symptoms caused by viral infection were much more severe and appeared 3 days earlier (Figure 3A,B), and CLCuMuV DNA levels were significantly higher in ATG5- and ATG7- silenced plants compared to control plants (Figure 3C).
evidence: Symptom incidence time course shows earlier symptom appearance in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 3B

claim: CLCuMuV DNA levels were significantly higher in ATG5- and ATG7-silenced plants compared to control plants
source: We observed that the leaf curl symptoms caused by viral infection were much more severe and appeared 3 days earlier (Figure 3A,B), and CLCuMuV DNA levels were significantly higher in ATG5- and ATG7- silenced plants compared to control plants (Figure 3C).
evidence: Real-time PCR quantification shows increased viral DNA accumulation in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 3C

claim: Silencing of GFP in N. benthamiana GFP transgenic line 16C had no effect on CA+β infection
source: By contrast, silencing of GFP in a N. benthamiana GFP transgenic line 16C had no effect on CA+β infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: GFP silencing did not affect viral symptoms or DNA accumulation, serving as a negative control, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Silencing of GAPCs delayed symptom development in plants infected by CA+β
source: Consistent with the observation that down-regulating cytosolic glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPCs) gene expression significantly activates autophagy (Han et al., 2015), we found that VIGS of GAPCs delayed symptom development in plants infected by CA+β (Figure 3D,E) and reduced viral DNA accumulation (Figure 3F).
evidence: Visual observation and symptom incidence data show delayed symptoms in GAPCs-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 3D,E

claim: Silencing of GAPCs reduced viral DNA accumulation
source: Consistent with the observation that down-regulating cytosolic glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPCs) gene expression significantly activates autophagy (Han et al., 2015), we found that VIGS of GAPCs delayed symptom development in plants infected by CA+β (Figure 3D,E) and reduced viral DNA accumulation (Figure 3F).
evidence: Real-time PCR quantification shows reduced viral DNA levels in GAPCs-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 3F

claim: Down-regulating GAPCs gene expression significantly activates autophagy
source: Consistent with the observation that down-regulating cytosolic glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPCs) gene expression significantly activates autophagy (Han et al., 2015), we found that VIGS of GAPCs delayed symptom development in plants infected by CA+β (Figure 3D,E) and reduced viral DNA accumulation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: Autophagy functions as an antiviral mechanism against CLCuMuV
source: These results suggest that autophagy functions as an antiviral mechanism against CLCuMuV.
evidence: Disrupting autophagy increases viral infection while enhancing autophagy reduces infection, indicating an antiviral role

claim: Interrupting the interaction between βC1 and ATG8 accelerated the occurrence of viral symptoms
source: Interrupting the interaction between βC1 and ATG8 accelerated the occurrence of viral symptoms and resulted in much more severe leaf curling symptoms than that caused by CA+β (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Visual observation and symptom incidence data show earlier and more severe symptoms with βC1V32A mutant virus, as shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Leaf curling symptoms caused by CA+βV32A appeared 3 days earlier than the symptoms caused by CA+β
source: Leaf curling symptoms caused by CA+βV32A appeared 3 days earlier than the symptoms caused by CA+β (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Symptom incidence time course shows earlier symptom appearance with βC1V32A mutant virus, as shown in Figure 4A-B

claim: Viral DNA accumulation was increased in plants infected by CA+βV32A versus CA+β
source: Moreover, we observed increased viral DNA accumulation in plants infected by CA+βV32A versus CA+β (Figure 4C).
evidence: Real-time PCR quantification shows higher viral DNA levels with βC1V32A mutant virus, as shown in Figure 4C

claim: The interaction of βC1 with NbATG8 is essential for the antiviral defense mechanism of autophagy against CLCuMuV infection
source: Since the V32A point mutation eliminates the interaction of βC1 with NbATG8f, these results suggest that the interaction of βC1 with NbATG8 is essential for the antiviral defense mechanism of autophagy against CLCuMuV infection.
evidence: Mutation that abolishes βC1-ATG8 interaction results in enhanced viral infection, indicating the interaction is required for antiviral defense

claim: YFP-βC1 accumulated in vacuoles in non-silenced control plants
source: As expected, we observed YFP-βC1 in the vacuoles in the non-silenced control plants. However, YFP-βC1 accumulated mostly in cytoplasm in ATG5- and ATG7- silenced plants (Figure 5A).
evidence: Confocal microscopy shows YFP-βC1 localization in vacuoles of control plants, as shown in Figure 5A

claim: YFP-βC1 accumulated mostly in cytoplasm in ATG5- and ATG7-silenced plants
source: As expected, we observed YFP-βC1 in the vacuoles in the non-silenced control plants. However, YFP-βC1 accumulated mostly in cytoplasm in ATG5- and ATG7- silenced plants (Figure 5A).
evidence: Confocal microscopy shows YFP-βC1 localization in cytoplasm when autophagy is disrupted, as shown in Figure 5A

claim: YFP-βC1V32A accumulated mostly in cytoplasm in all plants, regardless of whether ATG5/ATG7 was or not silenced
source: Similarly, YFP-βC1V32A also accumulated mostly in cytoplasm in all plants, regardless of whether ATG5 / ATG7 was or not silenced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confocal microscopy shows YFP-βC1V32A remains in cytoplasm regardless of autophagy status, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 resulted in more accumulation of YFP-βC1
source: In addition, silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 resulted in more accumulation of YFP-βC1 but not YFP-βC1V32A (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Western blot shows increased YFP-βC1 protein levels in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 5B

claim: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 did not affect accumulation of YFP-βC1V32A
source: In addition, silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 resulted in more accumulation of YFP-βC1 but not YFP-βC1V32A (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Western blot shows no change in YFP-βC1V32A protein levels in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 increased the accumulation of HA-βC1
source: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 increased the accumulation of βC1 but did not affect the level of βC1V32A mutant protein or GFP alone (in the control; Figure 5C).
evidence: Western blot shows increased HA-βC1 protein levels in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 5C

claim: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 did not affect the level of βC1V32A mutant protein
source: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 increased the accumulation of βC1 but did not affect the level of βC1V32A mutant protein or GFP alone (in the control; Figure 5C).
evidence: Western blot shows no change in HA-βC1V32A protein levels in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 5C

claim: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 did not affect the level of GFP alone
source: Silencing of either ATG5 or ATG7 increased the accumulation of βC1 but did not affect the level of βC1V32A mutant protein or GFP alone (in the control; Figure 5C).
evidence: Western blot shows no change in GFP protein levels in ATG-silenced plants, serving as a control, as shown in Figure 5C

claim: No difference in the RNA level of the βC1 construct was detected in NbATG5- or NbATG7-silenced plants
source: However, no difference in the RNA level of the βC1 construct was detected in NbATG5- or NbATG7-silenced plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR shows no change in βC1 mRNA levels in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: βC1 is targeted by autophagy for degradation
source: These results strongly suggest that βC1 is targeted by autophagy for the degradation, and the interaction of βC1 with NbATG8 is required for the autophagic degradation of βC1.
evidence: Increased βC1 protein accumulation without increased mRNA in autophagy-deficient plants indicates autophagy-mediated degradation

claim: The interaction of βC1 with NbATG8 is required for the autophagic degradation of βC1
source: These results strongly suggest that βC1 is targeted by autophagy for the degradation, and the interaction of βC1 with NbATG8 is required for the autophagic degradation of βC1.
evidence: βC1V32A mutant that cannot interact with ATG8 is not degraded by autophagy, indicating the interaction is required for degradation

claim: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms in plants infected by TYLCV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Visual observation and symptom data show more severe symptoms in ATG-silenced plants infected with TYLCV, as shown in Figure 6

claim: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 enhanced viral DNA accumulation in plants infected by TYLCV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Real-time PCR quantification shows increased TYLCV DNA levels in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 6D

claim: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms in plants infected by TYLCCNV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Visual observation and symptom data show more severe symptoms in ATG-silenced plants infected with TYLCCNV, as shown in Figure 6

claim: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 enhanced viral DNA accumulation in plants infected by TYLCCNV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Real-time PCR quantification shows increased TYLCCNV DNA levels in ATG-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 6C

claim: Silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms in plants infected by TYLCV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Visual observation and symptom data show reduced symptoms in GAPCs-silenced plants infected with TYLCV, as shown in Figure 6B

claim: Silencing of GAPCs reduced viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Real-time PCR quantification shows reduced TYLCV DNA levels in GAPCs-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 6F

claim: Silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms in plants infected by TYLCCNV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Visual observation and symptom data show reduced symptoms in GAPCs-silenced plants infected with TYLCCNV, as shown in Figure 6B

claim: Silencing of GAPCs reduced viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCCNV
source: Silencing of ATG5 and ATG7 caused more severe disease symptoms and enhanced viral DNA accumulation compared to the control, and silencing of GAPCs reduced the severity of viral disease symptoms and viral DNA levels in plants infected by TYLCV or TYLCCNV (Figure 6).
evidence: Real-time PCR quantification shows reduced TYLCCNV DNA levels in GAPCs-silenced plants, as shown in Figure 6E

claim: Autophagy may have evolved as a general antiviral mechanism against various geminiviruses
source: These results suggest that autophagy may have evolved as a general antiviral mechanism against various geminiviruses.
evidence: Autophagy affects infection by three different geminiviruses (CLCuMuV, TYLCV, TYLCCNV) in the same manner, suggesting a general mechanism

claim: Joka2 mRNA levels were significantly reduced in Joka2-silenced plants compared to non-silenced control plants
source: Joka2 mRNA levels were significantly reduced in Joka2-silenced plants compared to non-silenced control plants (Figure 7B).
evidence: Real-time RT-PCR shows reduced Joka2 mRNA levels in VIGS plants, as shown in Figure 7B

claim: Silencing of Joka2 had no effect on CLCuMuV infection of plants with CA+β
source: However, silencing of Joka2 had no effect on CLCuMuV infection of plants with CA+β (Figure 7C).
evidence: Visual observation and viral DNA quantification show no difference in infection between Joka2-silenced and control plants, as shown in Figure 7A,C

claim: Joka2-mediated selective autophagy is not involved in antiviral defense against CLCuMuV infection
source: These results suggest that Joka2-mediated selective autophagy is not involved in antiviral defense against CLCuMuV infection.
evidence: Silencing Joka2 does not affect viral infection, indicating this selective autophagy pathway is not involved in antiviral defense

claim: Autophagy is known to play an important role in disease resistance or susceptibility to various pathogens in plants
source: Autophagy is known to play an important role in disease resistance or susceptibility to various pathogens in plants (Han et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: Autophagy acts as a defense mechanism against some invading intracellular pathogens in mammalian systems
source: Autophagy acts as a defense mechanism against some invading intracellular pathogens in mammalian systems (Boyle and Randow, 2013; Randow and Youle, 2014; Paul and Münz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple publications cited in the manuscript

claim: Plant cells employ autophagy to defend themselves against several pathogens
source: Plant cells also employ autophagy to defend themselves against several pathogens (Han et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by previous publications cited in the manuscript

claim: Autophagy positively regulates plant resistance against necrotrophic pathogens
source: Autophagy positively regulates plant resistance against necrotrophic pathogens (Lai et al., 2011; Lenz et al., 2011; Kabbage et al., 2013) but negatively affects plant resistance against the biotrophic pathogen powdery mildew (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple publications cited in the manuscript

claim: Autophagy negatively affects plant resistance against the biotrophic pathogen powdery mildew
source: Autophagy positively regulates plant resistance against necrotrophic pathogens (Lai et al., 2011; Lenz et al., 2011; Kabbage et al., 2013) but negatively affects plant resistance against the biotrophic pathogen powdery mildew (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: Silencing of Joka2 enhances susceptibility to Phytophthora infestans
source: Furthermore, silencing of Joka2, encoding a selective autophagy cargo receptor for polyubiquitinated cargoes, enhances susceptibility to Phytophthora infestans although it is not reported whether disrupting autophagy has an effect on plant response to this pathogen (Dagdas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: Silencing of autophagy-related genes caused cell death induced by Tobacco mosaic virus to spread in inoculated leaves of N. benthamiana plants containing the TMV resistance gene N
source: In addition, silencing of autophagy-related genes caused cell death induced by Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) to spread in inoculated leaves of N. benthamiana plants containing the TMV resistance gene N but had no effect on plant systemic resistance against TMV (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: Silencing of autophagy-related genes had no effect on plant systemic resistance against TMV
source: In addition, silencing of autophagy-related genes caused cell death induced by Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) to spread in inoculated leaves of N. benthamiana plants containing the TMV resistance gene N but had no effect on plant systemic resistance against TMV (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: Autophagy can either facilitate or suppress viral infection in mammalian cells
source: Autophagy can either facilitate or suppress viral infection in mammalian cells (Orvedahl et al., 2010; Chiramel et al., 2013; Paul and Münz, 2016; Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple publications cited in the manuscript

claim: The VSR protein P0 from Polerovirus is thought to trigger the autophagic degradation of AGO1
source: Based on the data from autophagy inhibitor 3-MA treatment, the VSR protein P0 from Polerovirus is thought to trigger the autophagic degradation of AGO1, a component of the cellular RNAi-based antiviral defense machinery (Derrien et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript, though the evidence is based on chemical inhibitor treatment

claim: The VSR protein VPg from Turnip mosaic virus is reported to mediate the degradation of the cellular RNAi-based antiviral defense component SGS3, partially via autophagy
source: Similarly, the VSR protein VPg from Turnip mosaic virus is also reported to mediate the degradation of the cellular RNAi-based antiviral defense component SGS3, partially via autophagy (Cheng and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: 2b protein from Cucumber mosaic virus is thought to be targeted for degradation by autophagy through the calmodulin-like protein rgsCaM
source: Based on the data from an autophagy inhibitor treatment and silencing of an autophagy-nonspecific ATG gene Beclin 1, 2b protein from Cucumber mosaic virus is thought to be targeted for degradation by autophagy through the calmodulin-like protein rgsCaM (Nakahara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript, though the evidence is based on chemical inhibitor and non-specific gene silencing

claim: The in vitro application of an autophagy inhibitor wortmannin partially inhibited proteolysis of TYLCV proteins
source: In addition, the in vitro application of an autophagy inhibitor wortmannin partially inhibited proteolysis of TYLCV proteins (Gorovits et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication cited in the manuscript

claim: Autophagy genes are transcriptionally up-regulated by infection by some geminiviruses in plants
source: Further, autophagy genes are transcriptionally up-regulated by infection by some geminiviruses in plants (Ascencio-Ibáñez et al., 2008; Miozzi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by previous publications cited in the manuscript

claim: This study provides the first direct evidence that autophagy functions as an antiviral mechanism in compatible plant-virus interactions
source: To the best of our knowledge, in this study, we provide the first direct evidence that autophagy functions as an antiviral mechanism in compatible plant-virus interactions.
evidence: The authors claim this is the first direct evidence based on their use of specific ATG gene silencing and demonstration of effects on viral infection

claim: CLCuMuB βC1 is predicted to contain two ATG8-interacting motifs (AIMs)
source: CLCuMuB βC1 is predicted to contain two ATG8-interacting motifs (AIMs) (Kalvari et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction from a previous publication

claim: An approximately 11-amino-acid motif (LVSTKSPSLIK) comprising residues 30 to 40 of βC1 is responsible for the interaction of βC1 with NbATG8f
source: Interestingly, we found that an approximately 11-amino-acid motif (LVSTKSPSLIK) comprising residues 30 to 40 of βC1, but not the predicted AIMs, is responsible for the interaction of βC1 with NbATG8f.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from truncation mutants shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A point mutation at position 32 from valine to alanine in the ATG8-binding motif eliminated the βC1-NbATG8 interaction
source: Furthermore, a point mutation at position 32 from valine to alanine in this motif eliminated the βC1-NbATG8 interaction.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from multiple assays (GST pull-down, co-IP, BiFC) shown in Figure 1

claim: βC1 interacted with at least four NbATG8 homologs
source: In addition, we found that βC1 interacted with at least four NbATG8 homologs.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: ATG8 proteins interact with some cargo receptors, leading to autophagic degradation of the cargoes
